title: Gratitude for everything
tomorrow: Amira's packing. from up here, which way does everything face?

lines: A FOREHEAD BOWED TO OPEN HANDS.
cards: A living room with the furniture pushed back. Cushions on the floor, a tray of tea going cold, cousins with copies of the Qur'an open on their knees.

For days the family has been reading it through, each person taking a part, and tonight the youngest, a seven-year-old, reads the very last surah, an-Nas, in a careful voice. Then it's done. The whole book.

Someone exhales. And the grandmother, still healing from knee surgery, can't get down to the floor. So she leans forward from her chair as far as the knee allows, and bows her forehead to her open hands.

teach.h: SUJUD AL-SHUKR: THE BOW OF THANKS.
teach.b: What she's doing has a name: sujud al-shukr, the prostration of thanks. A hadith in Abu Dawud says that when something came to the Prophet ﷺ that made him glad, he would fall down in prostration, thanking God.

Not a speech. A body bending low. And when the knee won't bend, the tradition bends instead: the Prophet told a sick man to pray standing if he could, sitting if he couldn't, and on his side if he couldn't sit.

teach.h: AS LOW AS THE BODY ALLOWS.
teach.b: Gratitude goes as low as the body allows. The words that go with it are the first words of the Fatiha: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." Alhamdulillah.
All praise. Here's the surprising part, worth telling a friend tonight.

In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet said the believer's whole affair is a wonder, because all of it is good: when something good comes, they give thanks, and that is good for them; when harm comes, they're patient, and that is good for them too.
Gratitude for everything doesn't mean pretending the surgery didn't hurt, or the semester wasn't hard.
It means the whole journey, the hard parts included, can end with a forehead lowered.
Notice the senses of it: the cool of the floor, the smell of the carpet, the blood rushing to your face, your own breath close in your ears. Thanks you can feel.

how: When good news comes, many Muslims make a single prostration of thanks, sujud al-shukr, saying alhamdulillah; families often finish a khatm together with du'a and sweets.

o: thanking God for the whole journey, hard parts too
thanking God only once things go your way
a prayer said only at the end of Ramadan

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.
p: thanks in good, patience in harm
the last surah of the Qur'an

s: the Prophet would bow down in thanks when good news came
Abu Dawud 2774: he fell in prostration, thanking God.
in the hadith, only the good days count as good for a believer
Muslim 2999: thanks in the good, patience in the harm, and both are good.
if you can't kneel, you can't give thanks with your body at all
the Prophet told a sick man to pray sitting, or lying on his side (Bukhari 1117).

games.q: a friend gets a job offer and a breakup on the same day. what does the hadith of the believer's affair say?
o: thank God for the offer, and write off the breakup as bad luck.
both can be good: thanks for the one, patience in the other.
hold off on thanks until everything has settled down.
games.why: Muslim 2999: when good comes, thanks; when harm comes, patience; and both are good for the believer. gratitude for everything.

practice: If you can, kneel and lower your forehead to the floor; if not, bow your head to your open hands from where you sit.
Feel the floor or your palms against your forehead, and say alhamdulillah, or simply thank you, once for something good on this journey and once for something hard. Stay low until the time is up.

wordCard.voice: Gratitude for everything: alhamdulillah for the whole journey, the good as thanks, the hard as patience.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: all praise, said with your whole body, as low as it will go. Thirteen of fifteen.

sources.q: Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 2774 (the Prophet prostrated in thanks when something pleasing came to him)
Sahih Muslim 2999 (the believer's affair: thanks in good, patience in harm)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1117 (pray standing; if not, sitting; if not, on your side)
